suggestions.suggestion: Use storage repository abstraction with SQLite for mobile portability
suggestions.details: Q7 answer explicitly requires avoiding postgres and other non-portable databases per the storage-steer skill. Implement a repository interface pattern (as shown in storage-steer SKILL.md) so the storage backend can be PostgreSQL on the Vrooli server and SQLite on mobile/desktop. This is a fundamental architectural decision that must be baked in from day one — retrofitting it later would require rewriting every data access path. Use the storage-steer skill's dialect-switching pattern (PostgresTaskRepository / SQLiteTaskRepository) as the reference implementation.

suggestions.suggestion: Mirror web-console's Whisper integration pattern (local resource + streaming WebSocket)
suggestions.details: Q3 answer says to use the same approach as web-console. That means: local Whisper resource on port 8090, dual-mode transcription (WebSocket streaming for real-time partials + HTTP batch fallback), capability checking via whisper-stt probe, and ffmpeg transcoding to 16kHz mono WAV. The streaming mode is especially important for this app — users recording long voice thoughts need real-time feedback, not silence until recording stops. Reuse web-console's VoiceStreamProvider/WhisperProvider pattern on the frontend and the handleVoiceStreamWS handler on the backend rather than building from scratch.

suggestions.suggestion: Implement server-authoritative sync with optimistic local writes
suggestions.details: Q1 answer chose server-first. But the spec's offline-first requirement means the app must work without connectivity. The right pattern is: write optimistically to a local queue (IndexedDB or SQLite), sync to server when online, and resolve conflicts via last-write-wins with server as the authority. This avoids CRDT complexity while still enabling seamless offline use. Mark unsynced items visually so the user knows what hasn't been persisted to the server yet. Service worker handles background sync.

suggestions.suggestion: Use canvas virtualization from day one with spatial indexing
suggestions.details: Q5 answer chose virtualized canvas. For a mobile-first app with touch interactions, this needs a spatial index (quadtree or R-tree) to efficiently query which items are in the viewport. Libraries like react-flow already support viewport culling, but the data layer needs to support spatial queries too — store canvas positions in the database and index them. This prevents the common trap of building a simple canvas first and then struggling to bolt on virtualization when performance degrades at 100+ items.

suggestions.suggestion: Throttle periodic ghost-node generation to prevent LLM resource contention
suggestions.details: Q6 answer chose periodic generation when changes exist and previous generation isn't running. Since this app shares Ollama with other scenarios, unthrottled periodic LLM calls could starve other consumers. Add a configurable minimum interval (e.g., 30s default), a queue depth limit (max 1 pending generation), and respect Ollama's concurrent request limits. Also consider batching: if 5 items changed since last generation, process them in one LLM call with combined context rather than 5 separate calls.

suggestions.suggestion: Expose scheme data as a reusable scenario capability for other apps
suggestions.details: The export button currently targets web-console and agent-manager. But scheme data (structured thoughts with relationships, linked information, spatial layout) is a rich context source that any scenario could consume. Expose a read-only API endpoint (e.g., GET /api/v1/schemes/{id}/export) that returns the full scheme graph in a standardized format. This turns every scheme into a reusable knowledge artifact — future scenarios like report generators, presentation builders, or project planners could ingest scheme data directly. This aligns with Vrooli's compound intelligence vision where every scenario becomes a building block.
